questions.prompt: What problem does Chapter 6 attack first in its touch typing case study?
choices: The learner must replace a familiar bad pattern that still feels workable
The learner needs advanced typing shortcuts before basic practice can help
Typing is mainly limited by not owning the right keyboard

explanation.gentle: The chapter begins with habit repair, not total beginner confusion.
explanation.direct: Touch typing is difficult here because the old pattern already feels familiar enough to defend.
explanation.competitive: The first enemy is a bad habit that still pays rent.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 6 ask the learner to slow down on purpose?
choices: Because slower typing is always more accurate in the long run
Because the corrected pattern needs room before the old speed takes over
Because frustration disappears once the learner moves carefully enough

explanation.gentle: The slowdown matters because it gives the cleaner fingering a chance to happen consistently.
explanation.direct: The chapter treats the dip as structural: old speed keeps old error in charge.
explanation.competitive: You slow down to steal reps from the wrong habit.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter mean by corrected repetition?
choices: Typing many words until the hands eventually sort themselves out
Repeating the cleaner fingering often enough that it starts replacing the old motion
Alternating between old and new patterns to stay comfortable

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants reps that belong to the new pattern, not just more volume.
explanation.direct: Corrected repetition means the specific replacement keeps getting rehearsed after visible mistakes.
explanation.competitive: The right move has to own the reps.

questions.prompt: June can finish faster by returning to the old fingering in the keyboard lab. What response best fits Chapter 6?
choices: Protect a block where the corrected pattern matters more than short-term speed
Ignore the corrected drill until typing feels natural again
Switch back and forth constantly so frustration never builds

explanation.gentle: The chapter would keep one live block under the new pattern even if progress looks slower.
explanation.direct: This is the habit-repair choice in action: which pattern gets reinforced under real conditions?
explanation.competitive: She needs reps for the rewrite, not relief for the ego.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 6 treat frustration tolerance as part of the mechanism instead of as a side issue?
choices: Because the learner must interpret the dip without fleeing back to the smoother mistake
Because frustration itself teaches the fingers the correct positions
Because high frustration is the clearest sign that the best method was chosen

explanation.gentle: The learner can misread the ugly interval as proof the correction is wrong unless frustration gets a better meaning.
explanation.direct: The chapter builds emotional tolerance into repair because regression can be honest evidence of overwrite beginning.
explanation.competitive: If discomfort gets the final vote, the old habit wins again.

questions.prompt: When does slower practice become a trap in this chapter's logic?
choices: When it is paired with shorter sessions instead of one long drill
When it turns into careful movement without real pattern replacement
When it produces any temporary drop in fluency

explanation.gentle: Slowdown fails when the learner is not actually installing anything cleaner.
explanation.direct: The trap appears when calm pace disguises passive drift rather than useful overwrite.
explanation.competitive: Slow goes fake when the old structure still owns the keys.

questions.prompt: How would the chapter most likely apply to another familiar skill with a bad pattern in it?
choices: Accept a temporary dip, repeat the corrected version, and let stabilization serve that cleaner pattern
Move more slowly forever so the bad habit never gets a chance to return
Wait for rest alone to erase the old motion before practicing again

explanation.gentle: The broader lesson is habit overwrite through corrected repetition, not endless caution.
explanation.direct: Chapter 6 generalizes through temporary regression, specific replacement, and disciplined stabilization.
explanation.competitive: Same rule elsewhere: take the dip and feed the right move the reps.

questions.prompt: Malik predicts that one longer angry session will help more than shorter corrected rounds with return. Why does Chapter 6 reject that prediction?
choices: Because tired hands are always a sign that no learning happened
Because spacing and sleep can support a corrected pattern better than brute volume alone
Because long sessions are forbidden whenever a skill feels frustrating

explanation.gentle: The chapter allows effort, but it trusts corrected return more than sheer force.
explanation.direct: Consolidation matters because repeated corrected rounds can stabilize across time in a way one angry marathon often cannot.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's hardest warning about the temporary performance dip?
choices: That any visible regression means the learner chose the wrong fingering
That the dip can be misread as failure even when it is buying real replacement
That the learner should ignore all mistakes until consolidation has finished

explanation.gentle: The chapter is careful here: worse-looking performance can still be honest progress during overwrite.
explanation.direct: The danger is not the dip itself but the learner's urge to treat it as a verdict against correction.
explanation.competitive: The ugly interval can tell the truth while still feeling humiliating.

questions.prompt: If Chapter 6 repairs a motor habit through corrected repetition, what is the most natural bridge to Chapter 7?
choices: How the method changes when the next skill depends more on strategic complexity than on repetitive motor overwrite
How typing proves that all later skills should focus only on habit loops
How repetition can replace planning in every difficult domain

explanation.gentle: The next question is how the method behaves when the skill becomes more strategic and less repetitive.
explanation.direct: Chapter 7 can test whether the method still works once the challenge is pattern-rich decision making instead of keyboard rewiring.
explanation.competitive: The next battlefield is choice, not just reps.
